nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: American poet whose spare, myth-haunted lyrics of family, grief and the divine won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2020, the first American poet to be so honoured since 1993
biography: Louise Elisabeth Glück was born in New York City on 22 April 1943, the daughter of a businessman who had wanted to be a writer, and grew up on Long Island; she has said that her childhood was dominated by the death of an older sister before she was born and by a period of anorexia in her teens, during which she began psychoanalysis and, at seventeen, left school for it. She studied at Sarah Lawrence College and Columbia University, published Firstborn in 1968, and then wrote almost nothing for several years while teaching; The House on Marshland (1975) established the voice, and Descending Figure (1980), The Triumph of Achilles (1985, the National Book Critics Circle Award), Ararat (1990), The Wild Iris (1992, the Pulitzer Prize), Meadowlands (1996), Vita Nova (1999), The Seven Ages (2001), Averno (2006), A Village Life (2009), Faithful and Virtuous Night (2014, the National Book Award) and Winter Recipes from the Collective (2021) followed. Her essays are collected in Proofs and Theories (1994) and American Originality (2017). She taught at Williams College, was Poet Laureate of the United States from 2003 to 2004, and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2020 'for her unmistakable poetic voice that with austere beauty makes individual existence universal'. She died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 13 October 2023.
literary_profile: Poetry: Firstborn (1968), The House on Marshland (1975), Descending Figure (1980), The Triumph of Achilles (1985), Ararat (1990), The Wild Iris (1992), Meadowlands (1996), Vita Nova (1999), The Seven Ages (2001), Averno (2006), A Village Life (2009), Poems 1962-2012 (2012), Faithful and Virtuous Night (2014) and Winter Recipes from the Collective (2021). Essays: Proofs and Theories (1994), American Originality (2017).
stylistic_characteristics: Short, unrhymed and usually unpunctuated lines; a plain declarative syntax that turns, without warning, into myth; the first person used as a mask rather than a confession; sequences and recurring personae (the flowers and the gardener in The Wild Iris, the family of Ararat); and an ending that is usually a single hard sentence with no hedge in it.
intellectual_concerns: Family and its injuries, especially the father and the sister; grief and the work of mourning; the mythological and biblical stories that give private loss a public shape - Persephone, Orpheus and Eurydice, Abraham and Isaac; the garden and the seasons as a language for the divine; and, in the later books, old age, memory and the approach of death.
historical_significance: Glück is the central American lyric poet of the last half-century and the only American poet to have received the Nobel Prize since Toni Morrison's fiction was honoured in 1993. The Wild Iris is the book by which that award was most often justified, and it is the volume from which the Norton Anthology of American Literature takes 'Vespers'; Descending Figure, from a decade earlier, is the book in which the mythic method of her maturity first appears.
bibliographical_notes: The collections above come from Wikipedia's article on Glück, checked against the Nobel Prize citation and the contents of Poems 1962-2012; they were not checked against a printed bibliography, but the poetry collections are believed complete. Installment 10 records three Norton selections - 'The Drowned Children' and 'Descending Figure' from Descending Figure (1980) and 'Vespers' from The Wild Iris (1992) - so the essays and the later collections have no records.

birthplace: Rio Grande Valley, Texas, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Mexican American (Tejana); Chicana poet, essayist and theorist writing in English and Spanish
literary_identity: Chicana lesbian writer and theorist whose generically mixed Borderlands/La Frontera became a founding text of queer theory, Chicana feminism and US Third World feminism
biography: Gloria Evangelina Anzaldúa was born on 26 September 1942 in the Rio Grande Valley of south Texas, the eldest of six children of sharecropping Mexican American parents, and grew up between her family's land and the migrant labour camps of Texas. She took a BA in English from Pan American University and an MA in English and education from the University of Texas at Austin, and taught in the public schools of Texas before moving to California. With Cherríe Moraga she edited This Bridge Called My Back: Writings by Radical Women of Color (Persephone Press, 1981), the anthology that put the term 'women of color' into circulation and that she called a survival handbook for the women it named. Her major book, Borderlands/La Frontera: The New Mestiza (Aunt Lute Books, 1987), mixes autobiography, history, myth, poetry and theory in English, Spanish and Nahuatl to describe the border as an open wound and the mestiza consciousness as the answer to it. She was co-editor of Making Face, Making Soul/Haciendo Caras (1990) and returned to fiction with a children's book, Prietita and the Ghost Woman (1995). She took a doctorate at the University of California, Santa Cruz in 2002 and died of diabetes-related complications in Santa Cruz on 15 May 2004.
literary_profile: Borderlands/La Frontera: The New Mestiza (1987); This Bridge Called My Back (co-edited with Cherríe Moraga, 1981); Making Face, Making Soul/Haciendo Caras (edited, 1990); Prietita and the Ghost Woman (1995); and posthumous edited volumes of her writing on spirituality.
stylistic_characteristics: Genre-crossing and bilingual; chapters of autobiography, historical narrative, myth, poetry and theory set side by side without hierarchy; a first person that shifts between 'I' and 'we'; Spanish and Nahuatl left unglossed; and a style of sentence built to carry the emotions of fear, anger and survival together.
intellectual_concerns: The US-Mexico border as a lived wound rather than a line; mestizaje and hybrid identity; the taming of a wild tongue and the recovery of a mother tongue; the virgin of Guadalupe, Malintzin and Coatlicue as figures of female power; and the politics of writing as a queer Chicana.
historical_significance: Borderlands/La Frontera is the text through which Chicana feminism entered the American academy and is one of the founding documents of contemporary queer and postcolonial thought; its argument that identities are multiple and contradictory rather than singular is now a commonplace. The Norton Anthology of American Literature prints two chapters of it.
bibliographical_notes: The book list, the co-edited and edited anthologies and the dates are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page and the back matter of the 1999 Aunt Lute edition. Spanish-language and posthumously edited titles are named only where a catalogue entry could be checked.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African American; novelist, short-story writer, poet and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: African American novelist and essayist who reclaimed the Southern Black woman's inheritance in The Color Purple and coined 'womanist' as a term for Black feminist thought
biography: Alice Malsenior Walker was born on 9 February 1944 in Eatonton, Georgia, the eighth child of sharecrop tenants, and lost the sight of her right eye at eight in an accident that shaped her account of self-consciousness. She attended Spelman College and Sarah Lawrence College, where she finished her first collection of poems, Once (1968). Her early novels and stories - The Third Life of Grange Copeland (1970), In Love & Trouble: Stories of Black Women (1973) and Meridian (1976) - established her as a writer of the civil rights and Black feminist movements, and she taught and worked as a civil rights activist in Mississippi. The Color Purple (1982) won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award and was filmed by Steven Spielberg in 1985 and adapted for the musical stage in 2005. She published the essay collections In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens (1983) and Living by the Word (1988), the controversial The Temple of My Familiar (1989) and Possessing the Secret of Joy (1992), and a memoir, The Same River Twice (1996). She lives in Mendocino County, California.
literary_profile: Once (1968); The Third Life of Grange Copeland (1970); In Love & Trouble: Stories of Black Women (1973); Meridian (1976); You Can't Keep a Good Woman Down (1981); The Color Purple (1982); In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens: Womanist Prose (1983); The Temple of My Familiar (1989); Possessing the Secret of Joy (1992); and a body of poetry from Revolutionary Petunias (1973) to Taking the Arrow Out of the Heart (2018).
stylistic_characteristics: Direct, idiomatic Southern Black speech; a first person that moves between the spoken and the essayistic; letters and diary forms; and a plainness of syntax used to carry violent and tender material in the same sentence.
intellectual_concerns: The survival and creativity of Black women under racism and poverty; the mother's garden as an inheritance; sexual and domestic violence; the African American South; and, in the essays, the definition of a 'womanist' tradition against white feminism.
historical_significance: 'Everyday Use' is among the most anthologised short stories in American literature and is a standard text for teaching the conflict between a usable heritage and an ornamental one; 'In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens' gave the essay collection its title and made the phrase part of the vocabulary of Black feminist criticism. The Norton prints both.
bibliographical_notes: The principal novels, story collections and essay books are listed from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page; the poetry titles are given by span rather than individually, since the later volumes were not examined for this record.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African American; playwright writing in English
literary_identity: African American playwright whose ten-play Century Cycle dramatised a century of Black Pittsburgh and restored tragedy to the American stage
biography: August Wilson was born Frederick August Kittel Jr. on 27 April 1945 in the Hill District of Pittsburgh, the son of a German immigrant baker and an African American cleaning woman, and took his mother's name in 1965. He left school at fifteen and educated himself in the public library, then moved to St Paul, Minnesota, where he wrote plays for a theatre workshop. Ma Rainey's Black Bottom reached Broadway in 1984, and Fences, premiered at the Yale Repertory Theatre in 1985 and on Broadway in 1987 with James Earl Jones, won the Pulitzer Prize and the Tony Award. The ten plays that became the Pittsburgh Cycle or Century Cycle, one for each decade of the twentieth century, are Gem of the Ocean (2003), Joe Turner's Come and Gone (1988), Ma Rainey's Black Bottom (1984), The Piano Lesson (1990, Pulitzer), Two Trains Running (1992), Seven Guitars (1996), Fences (1987, Pulitzer), Jitney (1982), King Hedley II (2001) and Radio Golf (2005). He died of liver cancer in Seattle on 2 October 2005, a few months after Radio Golf opened.
literary_profile: The ten plays of the Pittsburgh/Century Cycle (1982-2005); Ma Rainey's Black Bottom (1984); Fences (1987); The Piano Lesson (1990); plus essays collected in The Ground on Which I Stand (1996), whose title piece attacks colour-blind casting.
stylistic_characteristics: Naturalistic dialogue built on the cadences of Black Pittsburgh speech; long arias of monologue inside domestic and workplace settings; a single unit set per play; and a symbolic structure - the fence, the piano, the train - carried by the objects on stage.
intellectual_concerns: The legacy of slavery and migration in the twentieth-century Black North; fatherhood and inheritance; the economics of Black labour; the blues and the 'blood's memory'; and the demand that African American experience be granted tragic rather than sociological form.
historical_significance: Fences is the most produced American play of its generation and won both the Pulitzer Prize and the Tony Award; its 2010 Broadway revival with Denzel Washington and the 2016 film have kept it in continuous performance. The Century Cycle as a whole is commonly described as the most ambitious dramatic project in American theatre, and Fences is the play through which the Norton represents it.
bibliographical_notes: The ten-cycle list, the premiere dates and the two Pulitzer Prizes were checked against the Wikipedia article and the Poetry Foundation author page; the 1985 Yale Repertory premiere of Fences and the 1987 Broadway run are given from the same sources.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American writer of the Vietnam War whose books treat memory, testimony and the impossibility of a true war story as their subject
biography: Timothy John O'Brien was born on 1 October 1946 in Austin, Minnesota, and graduated from Macalester College in 1968; he was drafted into the US Army that year and served in Vietnam in 1969-70 with the Third Platoon, Company A, Fifth Battalion, 46th Infantry, in Quang Ngai province. He began writing war stories on his return, and If I Die in a Combat Zone: Box Me Up and Ship Me Home appeared in 1973, followed by Northern Lights (1975) and Going After Cacciato (1978), which won the National Book Award and is built on a soldier's desertion and walk to Paris. The nuclear-war novel The Nuclear Age (1985) came before The Things They Carried (1990), his best-known book: a collection of linked stories whose narrator is named Tim O'Brien and which insists that its 'true' war stories are invented. In the Lake of the Woods (1994), Tomcat in Love (1998), July, July (2002) and Dad's Maybe Book (2019) followed. He holds a doctorate from the University of East Anglia and has taught at Texas State University.
literary_profile: If I Die in a Combat Zone (1973); Northern Lights (1975); Going After Cacciato (1978); The Nuclear Age (1985); The Things They Carried (1990); In the Lake of the Woods (1994); Tomcat in Love (1998); July, July (2002); and the memoir Dad's Maybe Book (2019).
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, reportorial sentence that declares its own unreliability; stories nested inside stories and told again with different outcomes; lists and inventories as a structural device; and a narrator who shares the author's name and contradicts his own testimony.
intellectual_concerns: The burden of memory and the guilt of survival; the difference between happening-truth and story-truth; cowardice and courage as a problem rather than a virtue; the weight of what soldiers carry, literal and moral; and the way a story is retold to keep the dead alive.
historical_significance: 'How to Tell a True War Story' is the metafictional centre of The Things They Carried and one of the most discussed short stories about Vietnam; its opening claim that a true war story is never moral is regularly quoted, and the book is a standard text in courses on American war writing and on historiography. The Norton prints the story on its own.
bibliographical_notes: The book list and the Vietnam service record come from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page and the 1990 Houghton Mifflin first edition's author note. The story's first appearance in Esquire is cited in the work record from the magazine's archives.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African American; poet writing in English
literary_identity: African American poet of the Vietnam War and of Black southern childhood, Pulitzer Prize 1994, whose music-inflected free verse made him one of the most influential American poets of his generation
biography: Yusef Komunyakaa was born James William Brown Jr. on 29 April 1947 in Bogalusa, Louisiana, and took the name Komunyakaa from his grandfather's family name. He served in the US Army in Vietnam from 1969 to 1970 as a correspondent and editor of the Southern Cross newspaper and was awarded the Bronze Star; he has said he did not begin to write about the war for more than a decade afterwards. He took degrees at the University of Colorado and Colorado State University and an MFA from the University of California, Irvine, and taught for many years at Indiana University and then at Princeton. Dedications & Other Dark Horses (1977), Copacetic (1984) and I Apologize for the Eyes in My Head (1986) came before Dien Cai Dau (1988), his Vietnam book, and Magic City (1992), which returns to Bogalusa. Neon Vernacular: New and Selected Poems 1977-1989 (1993) won the Pulitzer Prize and the Kingsley Tufts Award in 1994. Thieves of Paradise (1998), Talking Dirty to the Gods (2000), Pleasure Dome: New and Collected Poems 1975-1999 (2001), Taboo: The Wishbone Trilogy, Part One (2004) and Warhorses (2008) followed, along with the essay collection Blue Notes (2000) and the libretto for Scott Wheeler's opera Democracy.
literary_profile: Dedications & Other Dark Horses (1977); Copacetic (1984); I Apologize for the Eyes in My Head (1986); Dien Cai Dau (1988); Magic City (1992); Neon Vernacular (1993); Thieves of Paradise (1998); Talking Dirty to the Gods (2000); Pleasure Dome (2001); Taboo (2004); Warhorses (2008); The Emperor of Water Clocks (2015); and Blue Notes: Essays, Interviews and Commentaries (2000).
stylistic_characteristics: Free verse built on the cadence of blues, jazz and juke-joint speech; short lines with hard stops; concrete, often violent imagery; a syntax that withholds the subject; and long sequences that build single poems into a mythic anatomy.
intellectual_concerns: The Vietnam War and the survivor's memory of it, above all in 'Facing It'; Black southern childhood and labour; music as a mode of knowledge; the body, desire and violence; and the persistence of the mythological inside the everyday.
historical_significance: Komunyakaa is the most anthologised African American poet of his generation after the Black Arts writers, and 'Facing It' - his poem about the Vietnam Veterans Memorial - is one of the most widely taught poems about the war. The Pulitzer Prize for Neon Vernacular in 1994 confirmed a reputation built on Dien Cai Dau, and the Norton's four selections give him the largest block of any poet in the anthology's period.
bibliographical_notes: The collection list and the 1994 Pulitzer are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page and the Callaloo bibliography of his work (Michael Collins, Callaloo); first publication of individual poems is given in the work records only where the Callaloo bibliography or the collection's own notes state it.

birthplace: Stockholm, Sweden; raised in Queens, New York, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American (born in Sweden to Polish Jewish Holocaust survivors); cartoonist and graphic novelist writing in English
literary_identity: Cartoonist whose Maus turned the Holocaust memoir into graphic narrative and won the Pulitzer Prize, establishing the graphic novel as a literary form
biography: Art Spiegelman was born Itzhak Avraham ben Zeev Spiegelman on 15 February 1948 in Stockholm, where his Polish Jewish parents had gone after the war, and grew up in Rego Park, Queens, in New York. He began drawing professionally as a teenager and became part of the underground comix movement, drawing for East Village Other and co-founding Arcade with Bill Griffith in 1975. In 1980 he founded RAW with his wife Françoise Mouly, and in its pages he began Maus, a retelling of his father Vladek's survival of Auschwitz in which Jews are mice, Germans cats and Poles pigs. The first six chapters appeared as Maus I: A Survivor's Tale - My Father Bleeds History (Pantheon, 1986) and the rest as Maus II: A Survivor's Tale - And Here My Troubles Began (1991); the completed work was awarded a special Pulitzer Prize in 1992. He was the first cartoonist to be a regular contributor to The New Yorker, resigned over a pressure to tone down a Muhammad cartoon in 2003, and wrote Breakdowns: Portrait of the Artist as a Young %@&*! (2008) and the wordless MetaMaus (2011).
literary_profile: Maus I (1986) and Maus II (1991), collected as Maus: A Survivor's Tale (1992); Breakdowns (1977, expanded 2008); In the Shadow of No Towers (2004); MetaMaus (2011); and co-edited RAW (1980-91).
stylistic_characteristics: Anthropomorphic cartoon animals drawn in black and white ink; a frame narrative in which the son interviews the father; documentary panels of the camps set against domestic scenes in Rego Park; and a deliberately rough, hand-drawn line that refuses the polish of the museum.
intellectual_concerns: The Holocaust and its transmission to the second generation; the guilt of the survivor and of the son; representation itself, since the animal masks are an argument about how the Shoah can be told; and history as something that happens in a family.
historical_significance: Maus won the special Pulitzer Prize in 1992, the first ever awarded to a comic, and is the work that established the graphic novel as a subject of literary study; it is taught in history courses as well as literature courses, and 'Mousetrap' - the sixth chapter, printed here - is the chapter in which the wartime narrative and the father's present-day household are most tightly interleaved. The Norton's inclusion of it is a statement about the form.
bibliographical_notes: The two volumes, their Pantheon dates, the 1992 Pulitzer and the New Yorker resignation are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page and the publisher's edition notes; the page count and chapter numbering of 'Mousetrap' are from the 1986 volume.

birthplace: New York City, United States; raised in the Dominican Republic
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Dominican American; novelist, poet and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: Dominican American writer whose novels of immigration, bilingualism and the Trujillo dictatorship made her a central figure in Latina literature in the United States
biography: Julia Alvarez was born on 27 March 1950 in New York and taken to the Dominican Republic as an infant, where her father ran a farm and was involved in a plot against the dictator Rafael Trujillo. The family fled back to New York in 1960, ten months before Trujillo's assassination, and Alvarez grew up in Queens, learning English at school while Spanish stayed the language of home. She took degrees at Middlebury College and Syracuse University and worked as a migrant-labour-camp teacher, then taught English at Middlebury from 1988. Homecoming: New and Collected Poems (1984) came first, then the novel How the García Girls Lost Their Accents (Algonquin, 1991), which tells the story of four sisters backwards from their American adulthood to their Dominican childhood and made her reputation. In the Time of the Butterflies (1994) fictionalised the Mirabal sisters murdered by Trujillo, and ¡Yo! (Algonquin, 1997) returned to the García family, telling the second sister's story through the voices of everyone around her. In the Name of Salomé (2000), Saving the World (2006) and Afterlife (2020) followed, with the nonfiction Something to Declare (1998) and the middle-grade Tía Lola series.
literary_profile: Homecoming (1984); How the García Girls Lost Their Accents (1991); In the Time of the Butterflies (1994); ¡Yo! (1997); Something to Declare (1998); In the Name of Salomé (2000); Saving the World (2006); and Afterlife (2020), plus poetry from The Other Side/El Otro Lado (1995) onward.
stylistic_characteristics: Multiple first-person narrators, each with a distinct idiolect; non-chronological structures that run the immigrant story backwards; Spanish words left in the English text; and a comic voice that carries political material without solemnity.
intellectual_concerns: Immigration and the loss of a homeland; bilingualism and the taming of the tongue; the Trujillo dictatorship and the courage of ordinary women; sisterhood and family myth-making; and the position of the Latina writer inside the American academy.
historical_significance: 'The Mother' - the chapter the Norton prints - is the section of ¡Yo! in which Yo's mother narrates in the first person, and it is the piece most often taught from the novel because it dramatises the mother-daughter language gap in a single voice. Alvarez is one of the writers through whom the Norton represents the 1990s boom in US Latina fiction.
bibliographical_notes: The novels, the Algonquin dates and the biographical facts are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page; the poetry titles are given by span, since the individual volumes were not examined for this record.
